Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Can you tell from a cat’s face that it is in pain? Cats are famous for hiding that they feel unwell. Vets, it turns out, have learned to read it from the ears and whiskers. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Nvidia brings Jensen Huang back as its head, eleven days after he resigned. Nvidia, whose chips run almost all of today’s AI, has brought back its founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, eleven days after he resigned. The board says it voted unanimously after hearing from senior US government officials that his return poses no risk to national security; President Trump says he personally pressed for it. The company’s shares rose 31% in a day. An internal investigation and several official inquiries are continuing. Read more and the background.
  • OpenAI’s chief scientist proposes a line that no AI developer would cross until AI can be watched better. The chief scientist of OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has proposed that the leading AI developers agree on a shared limit that none of them would cross until the tools for watching what an AI does have improved. He suggests measuring progress by one simple number, how well a model guesses the next piece of unfamiliar text, and published OpenAI’s own figures. He expects new abilities soon that today’s tests may not even look for. It is one person’s proposal; no company has agreed to anything. Read more and the background.
  • The US and Chinese leaders agreed that a human must be involved in major military decisions made with AI, says the US Treasury Secretary. The US Treasury Secretary says Presidents Trump and Xi agreed at their meeting in China that a human being must always be involved in major military decisions made with AI. So far this is one official’s account of a conversation: Reuters mentions no written text and no confirmation from China, and it is unclear which weapons are covered. A day later, UN talks on “killer robots” ended without binding rules. Read more and the background.
  • An OpenAI model, working alone, writes a machine-checked proof of a 2006 theorem, taking a route of its own. An OpenAI model working entirely alone wrote a complete, computer-checked proof of a mathematical theorem first proved by a human in 2006, a testing company reports. The theorem was already known; what is notable is that the model took a different route from the published proof, because the usual tools were not available to it, and that it first honestly reported failure and succeeded only when sent back to try again. It took 94 minutes and about $22. Outside mathematicians have not yet reviewed it. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Riemann hypothesis proof: one more slow check passes, and Meta’s AI chief says the field is not ready for what follows, Report: Anthropic pays Elon Musk’s AI business about $3 billion a month to rent computers, ChatGPT’s everyday chat gets OpenAI’s newer model.

Answer to the question of the day. Yes, to a useful degree, and without any clever machine. An article in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok describes the Feline Grimace Scale, worked out by scientists at the University of Montreal. They watched 65 cats at the university’s veterinary hospital before and after a routine operation, filmed them, and compared what the faces looked like with and without pain; cats found to be in pain were given painkillers. Five signs turned out to matter: the ears, the eyes, the muzzle, the whiskers and the position of the head. A comfortable cat has ears pointing forward, open eyes, a relaxed round muzzle, loose curved whiskers and its head held above the shoulders. A cat in moderate or severe pain has ears flattened and turned outwards, squinting eyes, a tense, drawn-out muzzle, straight whiskers pushed forward and its head below the shoulder line. Each sign gets 0, 1 or 2 points. Scores given by different observers agreed with one another, and with older, slower ways of assessing pain in cats. The researchers also made a phone app for owners. One honest caveat for a digest about AI: the app does not recognise pain by itself. It shows you pictures and asks which looks most like your cat’s ears, eyes and muzzle right now, then adds up the score. The article files the subject under “computer vision”, and owners can upload a photo of their cat to add to the research collection, but the judging is still done by a human eye. Sistemny Blok, “How to tell that a cat is in pain: a guide to feline emotions from facial expression” (article in Russian).
